docs.title: ACE or Spring Boot? Where integration logic should live
docs.text:
Teams that have both IBM App Connect Enterprise and Spring Boot often ask the same question: should this go in ACE or in a service? Choosing badly leads to business rules hidden in integration flows, or hand-written plumbing that ACE would have handled for free.

Here's how I decide.

docs.title: Three layers, three jobs
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    C[Consumers: web, mobile, partners] --> G
    G[IBM API Connect<br/>security, plans, rate limits, analytics] --> S
    G --> A
    S[Spring Boot services<br/>business rules and data] <--> A
    A[IBM App Connect Enterprise<br/>connectivity and transformation] <--> B[ERP · legacy · SMS · IoT · partners]
  • API Connect is the front door: it publishes APIs, applies security policies, plans and rate limits, and gives you analytics.
  • Spring Boot services own the business domain: rules, validation and their own data.
  • App Connect Enterprise owns connectivity: protocols, formats, routing and mediation between systems.

docs.title: Put it in ACE when...
docs.text:
• You are translating between formats (JSON, XML, CSV, fixed-width) or protocols (HTTP, MQ, files, SOAP).
  • You are routing messages to different back ends based on content.
  • You are integrating packaged or legacy systems you can't change.
  • The logic is about how systems talk, not what the business decides.

docs.title: Put it in Spring Boot when...
docs.text:
• The logic is a business rule that the business will want to change and test.
  • It needs its own data and transactions.
  • It requires rich unit tests and fast developer iteration.
  • It is a capability other systems will call, such as "place order" or "calculate entitlement".

docs.title: Warning signs
docs.text: Symptom What it usually means ESQL with hundreds of lines of IF business conditions Domain logic has leaked into the integration layer. A Spring service full of SOAP clients and format mapping You are rebuilding an integration engine by hand. Each consumer calling back ends directly You are missing a gateway: security and visibility suffer. The same transformation copied into many flows Move it into a shared library.

docs.title: A simple rule
docs.text:
If the business would describe it, it belongs in a service. If only an integration engineer would describe it, it belongs in ACE. If it's about who may call what, and how often, it belongs in API Connect.

Keeping those boundaries clean is what lets an enterprise landscape keep growing without turning into a tangle.

Designing an integration architecture? I'd be glad to help.

docs.title: IBM App Connect Enterprise in practice
docs.text:
IBM App Connect Enterprise (ACE), the successor of IBM Integration Bus, is the integration engine inside IBM Cloud Pak for Integration. It connects systems that were never designed to talk to each other: an ERP, a REST API, a message queue, a file drop, a partner's SOAP service.

This is the mental model I wish I'd had on day one.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Concept What it is Message flow A graph of nodes: an input, some processing, one or more outputs. Application / REST API project A deployable unit that groups flows, maps and ESQL. Library / shared library Reusable code and schemas shared by several applications. BAR file The packaged, deployable archive (Broker ARchive). Integration server The runtime process that runs your deployed applications. Policy Externalized configuration: endpoints, credentials, MQ connections.

A typical flow looks like this:

flowchart LR
    I[HTTP Input] --> V[Validate]
    V --> C[Compute: ESQL transform]
    C --> R[HTTP Request: ERP API]
    R --> O[HTTP Reply]
    V -. failure .-> E[Error handler]

docs.title: Transforming messages with ESQL
docs.text:
The Compute node runs ESQL, ACE's language for reading and building message trees. Here a JSON order from a client is reshaped for a back-end system:

CREATE COMPUTE MODULE TransformOrder_Compute
  CREATE FUNCTION Main() RETURNS BOOLEAN
  BEGIN
    SET OutputRoot.Properties = InputRoot.Properties;

    SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.orderNumber = InputRoot.JSON.Data.id;
    SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.customerName = InputRoot.JSON.Data.customer.name;
    SET OutputRoot.JSON.Data.total = CAST(InputRoot.JSON.Data.amount AS DECIMAL);

    RETURN TRUE;
  END;
END MODULE;

For mapping-heavy work, the graphical Mapping node is often easier to maintain. I use ESQL when the logic has conditions, loops or lookups.

docs.title: Build and deploy from the command line
docs.text:
ACE 12 ships the ibmint tool, which makes builds scriptable and CI/CD friendly:

# Package an application into a BAR file
ibmint package --input-path ./workspace --project OrdersApp \
  --output-bar-file ./build/orders.bar

# Deploy it into an independent integration server's work directory
ibmint deploy --input-bar-file ./build/orders.bar \
  --output-work-directory /home/aceuser/ace-server

The same BAR file is then promoted through every environment, the same way you would promote a container image.

docs.title: Keep configuration out of the code
docs.text: Endpoints, credentials and connection details belong in policies, not hard-coded in flows. On Cloud Pak for Integration, policies and credentials are supplied as configurations attached to the integration runtime. The same BAR then runs in development, test and production with only the configuration changing.

docs.title: Lessons from production
docs.text:
• Design the contract first. Agree on the request, response and error formats before building the flow.
  • Handle errors deliberately. Wire the failure and catch terminals; never let a message disappear silently.
  • Log a correlation ID at every hop so one transaction can be traced across systems.
  • Keep flows small. Several focused flows are easier to test and operate than one huge flow.

docs.title: Debugging Pods on OpenShift: My oc Playbook
docs.text: When a pod is unhappy, OpenShift almost always tells you why. The trick is knowing which command shows the answer for which status. This is the playbook I follow, from the first command to the cluster-level tools.

docs.title: Always start with these three
docs.text:
oc get pods -o wide
oc describe pod <pod>                         # read the Events section at the bottom
oc get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

describe answers most questions on its own. The status column tells you where to look next.

docs.title: Pending: the pod was never scheduled
docs.text:
oc describe pod <pod> | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
oc describe quota
oc get limitrange
oc get pvc
Event message Meaning Fix Insufficient cpu / memory No node has room for your requests Lower requests or add capacity exceeded quota The project's ResourceQuota is full Raise quota or remove old workloads pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims PVC not bound Check StorageClass / oc get pvc didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector No node has that label Fix the selector or label a node

docs.title: ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull
docs.text:
oc describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Failed"
  • manifest unknown / not found: wrong image name or tag.

  • unauthorized: private registry without credentials:

    oc create secret docker-registry nexus-pull \
  --docker-server=nexus.example.com:8443 \
  --docker-username=ci --docker-password='***'
oc secrets link default nexus-pull --for=pull

  • x509: certificate signed by unknown authority: the cluster does not trust your registry's CA. An admin adds it via image.config.openshift.io/cluster (additionalTrustedCA).

docs.title: CrashLoopBackOff: it starts, then dies
docs.text:
The current container has probably just restarted, so its logs are empty. Read the previous one:

oc logs <pod> --previous
oc logs <pod> -c <container> --previous   # multi-container pods

Typical causes: missing environment variable or config, cannot reach the database, permission denied (see Why your container fails on OpenShift), or the liveness probe killing a slow-starting app.

When the container dies too fast to inspect, start a copy of it with a shell instead of its normal command:

oc debug deployment/orders-api
# inside: same image, env, volumes and SCC, but runs /bin/sh
env | sort
ls -la /app
java -jar /app/app.jar        # run it by hand and watch it fail

oc debug is the single most useful command on this page.

docs.title: OOMKilled
docs.text:
oc describe pod <pod> | grep -A3 "Last State"
#   Last State: Terminated
#     Reason:   OOMKilled
#     Exit Code: 137
oc adm top pods

The container used more memory than its limit. For Java, make the heap follow the limit with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 (details in Running Spring Boot on OpenShift), then raise the limit only if real usage needs it.

docs.title: CreateContainerConfigError
docs.text:
A referenced ConfigMap or Secret (or a key inside it) does not exist:

oc describe pod <pod> | grep -i "configmap\|secret"
oc get configmap,secret

docs.title: Running but 0/1 READY
docs.text:
The app is up but the readiness probe fails, so the Service sends it no traffic (and the Route shows Application is not available).

oc describe pod <pod> | grep -A3 Readiness
oc rsh <pod> curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness

Wrong path, wrong port, or a dependency the readiness check waits for.

docs.title: Inside a running pod
docs.text:
oc rsh <pod>                                   # interactive shell
oc exec <pod> -- cat /app/config/application.yaml
oc cp <pod>:/tmp/heapdump.hprof ./heapdump.hprof
oc port-forward <pod> 5005:5005                # attach a remote debugger locally

docs.title: When it is not your app: node and cluster
docs.text:
These need cluster-admin rights.

oc get nodes
oc adm top nodes
oc get clusteroperators                        # any DEGRADED=True?

oc debug node/<node>                           # privileged pod on the node
chroot /host
crictl ps | grep orders                        # containers as the runtime sees them
journalctl -u kubelet --since "10 min ago"

Opening a Red Hat support case? Collect everything at once:

oc adm must-gather            # cluster data into ./must-gather.local.*
oc adm inspect ns/orders-dev  # just one namespace

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Symptom First command Pending oc describe pod, oc describe quota ImagePullBackOff oc describe pod, check pull secret CrashLoopBackOff oc logs --previous, then oc debug OOMKilled (137) oc describe pod, oc adm top pods CreateContainerConfigError oc get configmap,secret Running, not Ready readiness probe path / port Route shows "not available" oc get endpoints Node problems oc debug node/…, oc get co

Save this table. Most incidents are one of these eight rows.

docs.title: OpenShift Routes: Edge, Passthrough and Re-encrypt TLS Explained
docs.text: A Route is how traffic from outside the cluster reaches your app on OpenShift. Creating one takes a single command; choosing where TLS ends is the decision that actually matters, for security, for features and for debugging. This post explains the three options and when I use each.

docs.title: How a request reaches your pod
docs.text:
Client ──► DNS *.apps.cluster.example.com
       ──► Router (HAProxy pods, the default IngressController)
       ──► Service  (selects pods by label)
       ──► Pod      (ready endpoints only)

The router runs HAProxy and watches every Route in the cluster. A wildcard DNS record points *.apps.<cluster-domain> at it, so any Route under that domain works without touching DNS. For a custom domain, point a CNAME at the router.

docs.title: Plain HTTP
docs.text:
oc expose service orders-api
oc get route orders-api
# orders-api-orders-dev.apps.cluster.example.com

Fine for a quick test. For anything real, pick one of the TLS types below.

docs.title: 1. Edge: TLS ends at the router
docs.text:
Client ══TLS══► Router ──HTTP──► Pod

oc create route edge orders-api \
  --service=orders-api \
  --hostname=orders.example.com \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key --ca-cert=ca.crt \
  --insecure-policy=Redirect
  • Without --cert, the router uses the cluster's default wildcard certificate.
  • --insecure-policy=Redirect sends http:// traffic to https://.
  • The router can read HTTP, so you get path-based routing, sticky sessions (cookies) and X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto headers.

Use it for: most web apps and APIs, when traffic inside the cluster network is acceptable in plain HTTP.

Spring Boot behind an edge route

Your app sees HTTP, so generated redirects and links may use http://. Set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework (or native) so Spring trusts X-Forwarded-Proto.

docs.title: 2. Passthrough: TLS goes all the way to the pod
docs.text:
Client ══════════TLS══════════► Pod   (router only reads the SNI hostname)

oc create route passthrough orders-api \
  --service=orders-api \
  --hostname=orders.example.com
  • The router never decrypts. It picks the backend using SNI from the TLS handshake.
  • The pod holds the certificate and serves TLS itself.
  • No path routing, no cookies, no forwarded headers: the router cannot see HTTP.

Use it for: mutual TLS where the app must see the client certificate (bank or partner integrations, for example IBM ACE or API gateways doing mTLS), non-HTTP protocols over TLS, and compliance rules that forbid decrypting at the edge.

docs.title: 3. Re-encrypt: TLS at the router, and again to the pod
docs.text:
Client ══TLS══► Router ══TLS══► Pod

oc create route reencrypt orders-api \
  --service=orders-api \
  --hostname=orders.example.com \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key

You get edge features (path routing, headers, cookies) and encryption inside the cluster. The router must trust the pod's certificate. The easy way is a service serving certificate, signed automatically by OpenShift's service CA:

oc annotate service orders-api \
  service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name=orders-api-tls

OpenShift creates the secret orders-api-tls (tls.crt, tls.key) and rotates it. Mount it in the pod and serve HTTPS on 8443. For a re-encrypt route with no destinationCACertificate, the router trusts the service CA automatically.

# Spring Boot: serve HTTPS with the mounted PEM files
server:
  port: 8443
  ssl:
    certificate: /etc/tls/tls.crt
    certificate-private-key: /etc/tls/tls.key

Use it for: regulated environments that require encryption in transit everywhere, while still needing router features.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text: Edge Passthrough Re-encrypt Where TLS ends Router Pod Router, then new TLS to pod Encrypted inside cluster No Yes Yes Certificate on Router Pod Both Path-based routing Yes No Yes Sticky sessions (cookie) Yes No Yes X-Forwarded-* headers Yes No Yes Client certificate (mTLS) seen by app No Yes No Complexity Low Medium Medium

docs.title: Useful annotations
docs.text:
# Long-running requests (default is 30s)
oc annotate route orders-api haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout=120s

# Load-balancing algorithm
oc annotate route orders-api haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance=roundrobin

docs.title: Route or Ingress?
docs.text: Both work. If you create a Kubernetes Ingress, OpenShift generates a Route from it, and you can choose the termination with an annotation such as route.openshift.io/termination: reencrypt. I use Ingress when the same manifests must run on other Kubernetes clusters, and Route when I need passthrough, re-encrypt or router annotations without workarounds.

docs.title: "Application is not available"
docs.text:
That page is the router saying: I have a Route, but no ready pod behind it. Check in this order:

oc get endpoints orders-api             # empty? nothing is ready or selected
oc get pods -l app=orders-api           # are pods Running and READY 1/1?
oc describe svc orders-api              # selector and targetPort match the pod?
oc get route orders-api -o yaml         # spec.to.name and spec.port.targetPort correct?

The usual causes: a failing readiness probe, a selector that does not match the pod labels, or a targetPort that points at the wrong port name. For passthrough and re-encrypt, also check that the pod actually serves TLS on that port.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
• Edge for most apps: simple, full HTTP features.
  • Passthrough when the app must own TLS, especially for mTLS.
  • Re-encrypt when you need router features and encryption everywhere; service serving certificates make it nearly free.

docs.title: Why Your Container Fails on OpenShift (and How to Fix It Properly)
docs.text: The image runs fine with docker run. It runs fine on your Kubernetes cluster. You deploy it to OpenShift and the pod goes straight into CrashLoopBackOff with Permission denied. The quick fix most people find on the internet is anyuid. Here is why that is usually the wrong fix, and what to do instead.

docs.title: The symptoms
docs.text:
nginx: [emerg] mkdir() "/var/cache/nginx/client_temp" failed (13: Permission denied)

Error: listen EACCES: permission denied 0.0.0.0:80

chown: changing ownership of '/data': Operation not permitted

Different apps, same cause: the image assumes it runs as root (or as one specific user), and on OpenShift it does not.

docs.title: What OpenShift actually does
docs.text:
Every pod is admitted through a Security Context Constraint (SCC). Ordinary workloads get restricted-v2, which:

  • runs the container as a random UID from a range reserved for the project;
  • adds the user to the root group (GID 0), but gives it no root privileges;
  • drops all Linux capabilities and blocks privilege escalation;
  • applies the default seccomp profile.

You can see the range assigned to your project:

oc get namespace orders-dev -o yaml | grep sa.scc
#   openshift.io/sa.scc.uid-range: 1000680000/10000

And check which SCC a running pod received and which user it runs as:

oc get pod orders-api-7d9c-xkq2 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.openshift\.io/scc}{"\n"}'
# restricted-v2
oc rsh orders-api-7d9c-xkq2 id
# uid=1000680000(1000680000) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1000680000

So the process is user 1000680000, which owns nothing in the image. Any directory owned by root:root with mode 755 is read-only to it. Ports below 1024 need a capability it does not have.

docs.title: Why not just grant anyuid?
docs.text:
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user anyuid -z default   # please don't

This lets every pod using the default service account in the project run as any user, including root. A container escape now starts from root on the node. On a shared or regulated cluster, it also tends to fail the next security review. And it hides the real problem: the image is not built to run unprivileged, which is a good practice on any platform.

docs.title: The proper fix: build images that run as any user
docs.text:
The rule is simple. Whatever the app needs to write must be owned by group 0 and group-writable. Because the random user is always a member of group 0, it gets access.

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal

RUN microdnf install -y nginx && microdnf clean all

# 1. Writable paths: group 0 + same permissions as the owner
RUN mkdir -p /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /run/nginx \
 && chgrp -R 0 /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /run/nginx /etc/nginx \
 && chmod -R g=u /var/cache/nginx /var/log/nginx /run/nginx /etc/nginx

# 2. Listen on an unprivileged port. In nginx.conf also set:
#    listen 8080;  and  pid /run/nginx/nginx.pid;
EXPOSE 8080

# 3. A numeric, non-root user (OpenShift will override the UID anyway)
USER 1001

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

Three habits cover most cases:

  1. chgrp -R 0 <dir> && chmod -R g=u <dir> for every path the app writes to.
  2. Listen on 8080 / 8443, never 80 / 443. The Service and Route map the public port.
  3. Use a numeric USER, never root, and do not chown at runtime.

Ready-made images

Many projects publish unprivileged variants: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged, Bitnami images, and Red Hat UBI images (ubi9/nginx-124, ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime, ubi9/postgresql-16) are built for the random UID out of the box.

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text: For persistent volumes, OpenShift sets an fsGroup from the project range, so the mounted volume is writable by the pod. Do not run an init container that chowns the volume: it needs root and will be rejected.

docs.title: Apps that need a username
docs.text:
A few tools (older Java libraries, SSH, some Python packages) call getpwuid() and crash when the UID has no entry in /etc/passwd. UBI-based images handle this. In your own images you can make /etc/passwd group-writable and add the entry in an entrypoint script:

#!/bin/sh
if ! whoami >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "app:x:$(id -u):0:app user:/app:/sbin/nologin" >> /etc/passwd
fi
exec "$@"

docs.title: When you genuinely need another SCC
docs.text:
Some workloads need more: a vendor image you cannot rebuild, a monitoring agent that reads host files. Then:

  1. Ask OpenShift which SCC would admit the pod:

    oc policy scc-subject-review -f deployment.yaml

  2. Create a dedicated service account and grant the SCC only to it, never to default:

    oc create serviceaccount legacy-app
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user anyuid -z legacy-app
oc set serviceaccount deployment/legacy-app legacy-app

  3. Document why, and add it to the list of exceptions you review regularly.

privileged should stay reserved for platform components such as CSI drivers and node agents.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Writable paths owned by group 0 with g=u permissions
  • App listens on a port above 1024
  • Numeric non-root USER in the Dockerfile
  • No runtime chown, no root init containers
  • Extra SCCs only through a dedicated service account, with a reason

Images that follow these rules run on OpenShift, on vanilla Kubernetes with Pod Security restricted, and on any hardened Docker host. Fixing the image once is cheaper than defending an exception forever.

docs.title: OpenShift Is Not Just Kubernetes: What You Actually Get
docs.text: "OpenShift is just Kubernetes with a Red Hat logo." I hear this often, and it is half true. Every OpenShift cluster is a conformant Kubernetes cluster: your Deployments, Services and ConfigMaps work as they do anywhere else. The difference is everything Red Hat decided you should not have to assemble yourself. This post walks through what those decisions are and when they are worth it.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
Plain Kubernetes gives you an engine. OpenShift gives you the car: engine, brakes, dashboard, seatbelts already fastened. You lose some freedom to pick parts, and you gain a platform that a small team can run in production.

Concern Plain Kubernetes OpenShift Exposing apps over HTTP(S) Choose and install an Ingress controller Routes + HAProxy router, installed Pod security Pod Security Admission, you set the policy SCCs, restricted by default Login & users Bring your own (OIDC, certs…) Built-in OAuth server (LDAP, OIDC, htpasswd) Image registry Install one Integrated registry + ImageStreams Building images External CI BuildConfig (S2I, Docker) in-cluster Monitoring Install Prometheus stack Prometheus + Alertmanager preinstalled Cluster upgrades Distro-specific Cluster Version Operator, one click / one command Node OS Any Linux RHCOS, immutable and managed by the cluster CLI kubectl oc (a superset of kubectl)

docs.title: 1. Projects instead of bare namespaces
docs.text:
A Project is a namespace with extras: a display name, a description, and a template that can attach default quotas, limit ranges and network policies the moment it is created. Developers can be allowed to create their own projects (oc new-project) without being cluster admins.

oc new-project orders-dev --display-name="Orders (dev)"
oc get project orders-dev -o yaml

docs.title: 2. Routes: ingress that is already there
docs.text:
Every cluster ships with an ingress controller (HAProxy) and a wildcard DNS name like *.apps.cluster.example.com. Exposing a service is one command:

oc expose service orders-api                          # plain HTTP
oc create route edge orders-api --service=orders-api  # HTTPS, TLS ends at the router

Routes also support passthrough and re-encrypt TLS, which I cover in OpenShift Routes explained. Standard Ingress objects still work: OpenShift converts them to Routes for you.

docs.title: 3. Secure by default (and why your image breaks)
docs.text:
This is the one that surprises people most. OpenShift does not let containers run as root by default. The restricted-v2 Security Context Constraint (SCC) runs each pod with a random, high user ID taken from a range assigned to the project, drops all Linux capabilities and blocks privilege escalation.

Images from Docker Hub that assume root (write to /var/cache/nginx, bind to port 80) fail on day one. That is a feature: it is the same hardening you should be doing anyway. The full story and the fix are in Why your container fails on OpenShift.

docs.title: 4. Authentication is built in
docs.text:
OpenShift runs its own OAuth server. Point it at LDAP / Active Directory, an OIDC provider such as Keycloak, or GitHub, and users log in to the console and the CLI with their existing accounts. Groups can be synced from LDAP and bound to roles.

oc login --web https://api.cluster.example.com:6443
oc whoami
oc adm groups new platform-admins
oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-group cluster-admin platform-admins

docs.title: 5. Registry, ImageStreams and Builds
docs.text: The cluster includes an image registry. On top of it, an ImageStream is a pointer to images (internal or external) that can trigger a redeploy when a tag changes. BuildConfigs build images inside the cluster from a Git repo or a binary upload, using Source-to-Image (S2I) or a Dockerfile. You do not have to use them (many teams build in GitLab CI and push to Nexus or Quay), but for small teams they remove a lot of plumbing. I compare the options for Java in Building Spring Boot images for OpenShift.

docs.title: 6. Operators run the cluster, and your middleware
docs.text:
OpenShift is managed by Operators: the Cluster Version Operator upgrades the whole platform, the Machine Config Operator manages node configuration, and so on. The same model is offered to you through OperatorHub: install Kafka (AMQ Streams), databases, Keycloak (Red Hat build of Keycloak), service mesh, GitOps (Argo CD) or IBM Cloud Pak for Integration with a few clicks, and the operator handles day-2 tasks like upgrades and failover.

oc get clusterversion
oc get clusteroperators   # the health of every platform component

docs.title: 7. Observability out of the box
docs.text: Prometheus, Alertmanager and dashboards for the platform are preinstalled. You can enable user workload monitoring to scrape your own apps (for example Spring Boot's /actuator/prometheus) with a ServiceMonitor, no extra Prometheus to run.

docs.title: When OpenShift is worth it
docs.text:
Choose OpenShift when:

  • you run in a regulated environment (banking, government, healthcare) that needs vendor support, certifications and hardened defaults;
  • the team is small and cannot afford to assemble and patch ten components by hand;
  • you run vendor software certified on OpenShift (IBM Cloud Pak, for example);
  • you need the same platform on-prem, in the cloud and at the edge.

Plain Kubernetes (or a managed service) may be enough when:

  • you are cloud-native on a single provider and happy with EKS / AKS / GKE;
  • you want full control over every component;
  • budget is the main constraint (OpenShift is a subscription; OKD is the free upstream).

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text:
OpenShift's value is not one big feature. It is dozens of decisions already made: secure defaults, integrated login, routing, registry, monitoring and push-button upgrades. If those are decisions your team would otherwise make (and maintain) itself, OpenShift saves real time. If not, plain Kubernetes is a perfectly good engine.

docs.title: Securing Spring Boot APIs with Keycloak
docs.text: When an organization runs many services, each one managing its own users quickly becomes a security problem. Keycloak centralizes authentication. Your Spring Boot APIs only need to check the token that comes with each request.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
The client (an Angular app, a mobile app or another service) gets an access token from Keycloak and sends it in the Authorization: Bearer ... header. The API validates the token's signature with Keycloak's public keys. It never sees a password.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client app
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant A as Spring Boot API
    C->>K: Log in (OIDC)
    K->>C: Access token (JWT)
    C->>A: GET /api/orders + Bearer token
    A->>K: Fetch signing keys (cached)
    A->>C: 200 OK, or 401 / 403

docs.title: 1. Configure Keycloak
docs.text:
In your realm:

  1. Create a client for the front end, e.g. orders-ui (public client, standard flow with PKCE).
  2. Create realm roles such as orders.read and orders.write, and assign them to users or groups.
  3. If users live in a directory, add LDAP user federation to the realm.

docs.title: 2. Make the API a resource server
docs.text:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://sso.example.com/realms/company

With issuer-uri set, Spring discovers the signing keys and checks the token's signature, expiry and issuer automatically.

docs.title: 3. Map Keycloak roles to Spring authorities
docs.text:
Keycloak puts realm roles inside a realm_access.roles claim, which Spring does not read by default. A small converter fixes that:

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth
                .jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(keycloakRoles())))
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS));
        return http.build();
    }

    private JwtAuthenticationConverter keycloakRoles() {
        var converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
        converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(jwt -> {
            Map<String, Object> realmAccess = jwt.getClaimAsMap("realm_access");
            if (realmAccess == null) return List.of();
            @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
            var roles = (Collection<String>) realmAccess.getOrDefault("roles", List.of());
            return roles.stream()
                .map(role -> (GrantedAuthority) new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + role))
                .toList();
        });
        return converter;
    }
}

Now authorization reads like the business rules:

@GetMapping("/api/orders")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('orders.read')")
List<Order> list() { ... }

docs.title: Mistakes I see most often
docs.text:
• Wildcard redirect URIs such as * on clients. Always list exact URLs.
  • Trusting the token without checking the audience when many clients share a realm. Add an audience mapper in Keycloak and validate it in the API.
  • Long-lived access tokens. Keep them short (minutes) and rely on refresh tokens.
  • Doing all authorization in Keycloak. Use roles as input, but keep business rules such as "a user can only see their own orders" in the service.

docs.title: Service-to-service calls
docs.text:
For backend-to-backend calls, use the client credentials grant: the calling service gets its own token with its own roles, so every call is authenticated and auditable.

docs.title: Running Spring Boot on OpenShift
docs.text: Getting a Spring Boot service to start on OpenShift takes five minutes. Getting it to behave well in production (rolling updates without errors, sensible memory use, configuration per environment) takes a few deliberate choices. This is the checklist I follow.

docs.title: 1. Build an image that runs as any user
docs.text:
OpenShift runs containers with a random, non-root user ID that belongs to the root group. Images that assume root, or write to directories only their owner can write to, fail at startup.

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar app.jar
RUN chgrp -R 0 /app && chmod -R g=u /app
USER 1001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

Two details matter here:

  • Port 8080. Ports below 1024 need privileges the container won't have.
  • -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. The JVM sizes its heap from the container's memory limit, leaving room for metaspace, threads and native memory. Without it you get either a wasted limit or an OOMKilled pod.

Tip

Red Hat's UBI OpenJDK images (ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime) are built for this environment and are a good choice when you need a supported base image.

docs.title: 2. Use Actuator for health probes
docs.text:
Spring Boot Actuator exposes separate liveness and readiness groups. They are enabled automatically when the app detects Kubernetes, and you can turn them on explicitly:

# application.yaml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info

# Deployment
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 20

Keep the liveness check simple. If it depends on the database, a short database outage restarts every pod at once and turns a small incident into a big one.

docs.title: 3. Shut down gracefully
docs.text:
During a rolling update, OpenShift sends SIGTERM to the old pod. Let in-flight requests finish:

server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s

Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds on the pod higher than that timeout.

docs.title: 4. Configuration from the platform
docs.text:
Build one image and promote it through every environment. Everything that changes per environment comes from OpenShift:

What Where URLs, feature flags, log levels ConfigMap as environment variables Passwords, client secrets, keys Secret TLS for the public endpoint Route with edge or re-encrypt termination

Spring's relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url, so no code changes are needed.

oc create configmap orders-config --from-literal=SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
oc set env deployment/orders-api --from=configmap/orders-config
oc create route edge orders-api --service=orders-api

docs.title: 5. Set requests and limits
docs.text:
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
  limits:   { memory: 1Gi }

Requests let the scheduler place pods sensibly. A memory limit protects the node. I usually avoid a tight CPU limit for JVM services because throttling slows startup and garbage collection.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Non-root image listening on 8080
  • Heap sized with MaxRAMPercentage
  • Readiness and liveness probes on Actuator
  • Graceful shutdown configured
  • Config in ConfigMaps, secrets in Secrets
  • Resource requests and a memory limit

docs.title: Building Spring Boot Images for OpenShift: Dockerfile, S2I or Jib?
docs.text: There are at least four reasonable ways to get a Spring Boot JAR running as an image on OpenShift. They all work. They differ in where the build runs, who controls the base image and how much CI you need. Here is each one with real commands, and how I pick between them.

docs.title: Option 1: Dockerfile, built in CI, pushed to a registry
docs.text:
The most portable approach. GitLab CI (or Jenkins, GitHub Actions) builds the image and pushes it to Nexus, Quay or Harbor; OpenShift only pulls and runs it.

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21 AS build
USER 0
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar /deployments/app.jar
EXPOSE 8080

# .gitlab-ci.yml (simplified)
build-image:
  image: quay.io/buildah/stable
  script:
    - buildah bud -t $REGISTRY/orders-api:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA .
    - buildah push $REGISTRY/orders-api:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

deploy:
  image: registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cli
  script:
    - oc login --token=$OC_TOKEN --server=$OC_SERVER
    - oc set image deployment/orders-api orders-api=$REGISTRY/orders-api:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
    - oc rollout status deployment/orders-api

The UBI OpenJDK runtime image runs /deployments/*.jar automatically, works with OpenShift's random UID, and sizes the heap from the container limit.

Good: same image everywhere, full control, no build load on the cluster. Cost: you maintain the CI pipeline and the registry.

docs.title: Option 2: Docker strategy, built inside OpenShift
docs.text:
Same Dockerfile, but OpenShift builds it with a BuildConfig and stores the result in the internal registry.

oc new-build --strategy=docker --binary --name=orders-api
oc start-build orders-api --from-dir=. --follow
oc new-app orders-api                  # first deploy
oc expose service orders-api

Good: no registry or Docker daemon needed outside the cluster. Handy for small teams and disconnected environments. Cost: builds use cluster CPU and memory; the cluster admin may restrict the Docker strategy.

docs.title: Option 3: Source-to-Image (S2I)
docs.text:
No Dockerfile at all. You give OpenShift source code (or a JAR), and a builder image knows how to build and run Java.

From Git:

oc new-app registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21~https://gitlab.example.com/team/orders-api.git \
  --name=orders-api

Or from a JAR you already built:

oc new-build registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21 --binary --name=orders-api
./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
oc start-build orders-api --from-file=target/orders-api.jar --follow

Good: developers only push code; Red Hat maintains the base image, so rebuilding picks up security patches. Cost: less control over the image layout; OpenShift-specific.

docs.title: Option 4: Jib, no Dockerfile and no Docker daemon
docs.text:
Jib, a Maven/Gradle plugin from Google, builds layered images directly from the build tool. Dependencies, resources and classes go in separate layers, so a code change pushes only a few KB.

<plugin>
  <groupId>com.google.cloud.tools</groupId>
  <artifactId>jib-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.4</version>
  <configuration>
    <from><image>registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/openjdk-21-runtime</image></from>
    <to><image>nexus.example.com:8443/team/orders-api</image></to>
    <container>
      <user>185</user>
      <ports><port>8080</port></ports>
    </container>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

./mvnw compile jib:build -Djib.to.tags=$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

Good: fast incremental builds, reproducible, runs in any CI container without privileges. Cost: Java-only; you still need a registry.

Cloud Native Buildpacks

./mvnw spring-boot:build-image (Paketo Buildpacks) is a fifth option with good defaults. It needs a Docker-compatible daemon at build time, which is often the deciding factor in CI.

docs.text: Dockerfile in CI Docker strategy S2I Jib Build runs in CI OpenShift OpenShift CI / laptop Needs Dockerfile Yes Yes No No Needs Docker daemon No (Buildah/Kaniko) No No No External registry Yes No No Yes Portable to other K8s Yes Image only Image only Yes Incremental speed Good (layer cache) Good Medium Best Base image patching You You Red Hat You

docs.title: Triggering the deploy
docs.text:
Whatever builds the image, roll it out in one of two ways:

# Explicit: CI sets the new tag (clear audit trail, easy rollback)
oc set image deployment/orders-api orders-api=nexus.example.com:8443/team/orders-api:1.4.2
oc rollout status deployment/orders-api
oc rollout undo deployment/orders-api        # if needed

# Automatic: redeploy when an ImageStream tag changes (in-cluster builds)
oc set triggers deployment/orders-api --from-image=orders-api:latest -c orders-api

docs.title: How I choose
docs.text:
• Team already has GitLab CI and a registry: Dockerfile (or Jib) in CI, oc set image to deploy. Portable, auditable, and the cluster only runs workloads.
  • Small team, no external registry, or a disconnected cluster: binary S2I with the UBI OpenJDK builder. Least to maintain.
  • Many Java microservices with frequent builds: Jib, for layer reuse and speed.

Whichever you choose, the runtime rules stay the same: non-root image, port 8080, probes on Actuator, graceful shutdown. They are all in Running Spring Boot on OpenShift.

docs.title: Keycloak Laravel Auth
docs.text:
GitHub Packagist Get started

A complete Keycloak integration for Laravel 11, 12 and 13. It covers what a backend usually needs from an identity provider: browser single sign-on, authenticating API calls, roles and permissions, calling other services, and managing users. All of it goes through one facade.

// Protect an API: the token is verified offline, no call to Keycloak
Route::middleware(['keycloak.api', 'keycloak.role:admin'])->get('/orders', OrderController::class);

// Read the current token anywhere
Keycloak::token()->hasRole('billing:invoice-viewer');

// Call another microservice with a cached service-account token
Http::withKeycloakToken('api')->get('https://orders.internal/api/orders');

// Manage users, roles and groups
$id = Keycloak::users()->create(['username' => 'jane', 'email' => 'jane@example.com', 'password' => 'S3cret!']);
Keycloak::users()->assignRealmRoles($id, ['editor']);

docs.title: Why this package
docs.text:
• Fast by design. Access tokens are verified offline against the realm's public keys, which are cached in your cache store and in memory. A protected API request makes no network call. A token is verified once per process, admin and service tokens are reused for their real lifetime, and provisioning skips the database write while a user's claims are unchanged.
  • Secure defaults. It checks the signature, exp/nbf with leeway, issuer, audience and token type, and only accepts allow-listed algorithms, so none and HMAC tokens are rejected. Key rotation is picked up automatically. The browser login uses PKCE and regenerates the session.
  • Everything a backend needs. Browser SSO, a keycloak auth guard, role, scope, group and UMA permission checks, the main OIDC grants, token exchange, and the Admin REST API (users, roles, groups, clients, events).
  • Works with Laravel's own tools: guards, $request->user(), middleware, gates, @can, Blade directives, events, the Http client and Artisan.
  • Built to test. Keycloak::fake() signs real RS256 tokens locally, so your feature tests need no Keycloak server.
  • Backward compatible with the 1.x services, middleware and facade.

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text:
Keycloak::admin($guard) is a client for the Keycloak Admin REST API of a guard's realm. It authenticates with the service account of the admin guard (see Installation → Setting up Keycloak).

use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Facades\Keycloak;

Keycloak::users();          // = Keycloak::admin()->users(), default guard's realm
Keycloak::users('partners');// another realm
Keycloak::roles();
Keycloak::groups();
Keycloak::clients();
Keycloak::admin()->realm();
  • The admin token is fetched once, cached for its real lifetime and shared by all calls. A 401 refreshes it and retries once.
  • Methods return Keycloak's JSON representations as plain arrays.
  • Failures throw Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Exceptions\AdminApiException (status(), errorDescription(), response()). find()-style methods return null on 404.
  • Client UUID lookups are cached, so you always pass the human clientId ("billing"), never the UUID.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
$users = Keycloak::users();

// Create: snake_case or Keycloak camelCase keys. Returns the new id.
$id = $users->create([
    'username' => 'jane',
    'email' => 'jane@example.com',
    'first_name' => 'Jane',
    'last_name' => 'Doe',
    'email_verified' => true,
    'enabled' => true,                      // default true
    'attributes' => ['department' => 'IT'], // values become arrays
    'groups' => ['/staff'],
    'required_actions' => ['VERIFY_EMAIL'],
    'password' => 'S3cret!',
    'temp_password' => true,                // force a change at first login
]);

$users->update($id, ['first_name' => 'Janet']);  // partial update
$users->setAttributes($id, ['department' => 'HR', 'legacy_id' => null]); // merge; null removes
$users->disable($id);
$users->enable($id);
$users->resetPassword($id, 'N3w-pass', temporary: false);
$users->delete($id);

$users->removeClientRoles($id, 'billing', ['invoice-viewer']);

docs.title: Keeping the local users table in sync
docs.text:
The 1.x KeycloakUsersService is still available. It calls the Admin API and updates the local user row in one step:

use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Services\KeycloakUsersService;

$user = KeycloakUsersService::guard('web')->create([...]);   // returns the KCUserModel
KeycloakUsersService::guard('web')->createOrUpdate(['email' => 'jane@example.com', /* ... */]);
KeycloakUsersService::guard('web')->setStatus($keycloakId, false);

docs.title: Example: invite a user
docs.text:
public function invite(InviteRequest $request)
{
    $users = Keycloak::users();

    $id = $users->create([
        'username' => $request->email,
        'email' => $request->email,
        'first_name' => $request->first_name,
        'last_name' => $request->last_name,
        'required_actions' => ['VERIFY_EMAIL', 'UPDATE_PASSWORD'],
    ]);

    $users->assignRealmRoles($id, [$request->role]);
    $users->executeActionsEmail($id, ['VERIFY_EMAIL', 'UPDATE_PASSWORD'], lifespan: 86400, redirectUri: url('/'));

    return response()->json(['id' => $id], 201);
}

docs.title: API authentication
docs.text:
Your SPA, mobile app or another service gets an access token from Keycloak and sends it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The package verifies the token offline against the realm's cached public keys. A request needs no call to Keycloak and no database query, unless you provision users.

There are two ways to plug it in. Both share the same validation, caching and user resolution.

docs.title: Option 1: the keycloak.api middleware
docs.text:
// routes/api.php
Route::middleware('keycloak.api')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/me', fn (Request $request) => $request->user());
    Route::apiResource('orders', OrderController::class);
});

Route::middleware('keycloak.api:partners')->group(/* tokens of the "partners" guard */);

When nothing is passed it uses the api guard if you configured one, otherwise the default guard.

Failures return JSON:

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer

{ "error": "Invalid or expired token" }

With APP_DEBUG=true the response also contains a message with the exact reason (expired, wrong issuer, audience...).

docs.title: Option 2: the keycloak auth guard
docs.text:
Register a guard in config/auth.php:

'guards' => [
    'web' => ['driver' => 'session', 'provider' => 'users'],

    'api' => [
        'driver' => 'keycloak',
        'keycloak' => 'api',      // which package guard (realm + client) to verify against
        // 'provision' => false,  // override provisioning for this guard
    ],
],

Then use Laravel's own auth middleware and helpers:

Route::middleware('auth:api')->get('/me', fn () => auth('api')->user());

auth('api')->check();
auth('api')->id();                        // Keycloak subject (stateless) or local id
auth('api')->token();                     // KeycloakToken
auth('api')->hasRole('admin');
auth('api')->validate(['token' => $jwt]); // check without logging in

Unauthenticated requests go through Laravel's normal AuthenticationException handling (JSON 401 for API requests). The guard is safe for Laravel Octane: it is reset for every request.

docs.title: Users: stateless or database
Custom user resolution
docs.text:
Take full control over how a token becomes a user, for example to look up a tenant or deny unknown users:

// AppServiceProvider::boot()
use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Facades\Keycloak;
use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Token\KeycloakToken;

Keycloak::resolveUserUsing(function (KeycloakToken $token, string $guard) {
    return User::firstWhere('keycloak_id', $token->subject()); // null = unauthenticated
});

docs.title: Reading the token
docs.text:
use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Facades\Keycloak;

$token = Keycloak::token();     // current request token (or inject KeycloakToken)

$token->subject();              // user id
$token->email();
$token->username();
$token->azp();                  // client the token was issued to
$token->roles();                // realm + guard-client roles
$token->scopes();
$token->groups();
$token->expiresAt();            // CarbonImmutable
$token->claim('tenant.id');     // any claim, dot notation
$token->jwt();                  // raw token, e.g. to forward it

public function index(KeycloakToken $token) { /* injected from the container */ }

docs.title: Validating tokens yourself
docs.text:
For queues, WebSockets, gRPC or anywhere outside HTTP middleware:

$token = Keycloak::validate($jwt, 'api');   // throws TokenValidationException
$token = Keycloak::check($jwt, 'api');      // or returns null
$token = Keycloak::decode($jwt);            // claims only, NO verification

What is verified:

  • Signature against the realm's JWKS, with only allow-listed algorithms.
  • Expiry and not-before, with token.leeway seconds of clock skew.
  • Issuer: {base_url}/realms/{realm} or a configured public issuer.
  • Audience: when the guard has audience, it must be in aud or azp.
  • Type: typ must be Bearer, so refresh and ID tokens are refused.

docs.title: Performance notes
docs.text:
• Realm keys are cached in your cache store (token.jwks_ttl, 1 day) and memoized in-process.
  • When a token is signed with an unknown key id (Keycloak rotated its keys), the keys are downloaded again, at most once per token.jwks_refresh_cooldown seconds. Forged tokens can't be used to flood Keycloak with requests.
  • The same token is verified only once per process (up to 256 recent tokens are memoized; the expiry is re-checked on every use).
  • Use a shared cache (Redis) in production so every server and worker reuses the same keys and tokens.

docs.title: Docker, Kubernetes and public URLs
docs.text:
Inside a cluster your app often reaches Keycloak at an internal URL (http://keycloak:8080), while tokens are issued with the public URL as iss (https://sso.example.com/realms/my-realm). Keep the internal URL for HTTP calls and trust the public issuer:

KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL=http://keycloak:8080
KEYCLOAK_ISSUER=https://sso.example.com    # realm path is added automatically

You can also set issuer per guard (string or array) in the config.

docs.title: Microservices
docs.text:
A typical setup: each service verifies incoming tokens with keycloak.api, and calls other services either on behalf of the user (forward the token) or as itself (service account):

// forward the caller's token
Http::withKeycloakUserToken()->get('http://inventory/api/stock');

// call as this service (client credentials, cached until it expires)
Http::withKeycloakToken('api')->post('http://billing/api/invoices', $payload);

See OIDC & service tokens for token exchange and scopes.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Event When TokenValidated a bearer token was accepted ($token, $guard) TokenValidationFailed a bearer token was rejected ($exception, $guard, $request), useful for auditing and alerts UserProvisioned the local user row was created or changed

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: All checks read the current request's token: the verified bearer token on API routes, or the session token on web routes. They make no network call, except UMA permissions.

docs.title: Role semantics
docs.text:
You write Matches admin the realm role admin or the role admin of the guard's client (and of the token's azp) billing:invoice-viewer the role invoice-viewer of the client billing App\Enums\Role::Admin backed enums use their value, pure enums their name

The "guard's client" can be changed with roles.clients or the guard's role_clients (configuration).

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
// at least one of the roles
Route::middleware(['keycloak.api', 'keycloak.role:admin,editor'])->group(/* ... */);

// all of the roles
Route::middleware(['keycloak.api', 'keycloak.roles:admin,auditor'])->group(/* ... */);

// client role
Route::middleware(['keycloak.api', 'keycloak.role:billing:invoice-viewer'])->get('/invoices', /* ... */);

// at least one of the scopes
Route::middleware(['keycloak.api', 'keycloak.scope:orders:read,orders:write'])->get('/orders', /* ... */);

// Keycloak Authorization Services (UMA), all listed permissions
Route::middleware(['keycloak.api', 'keycloak.permission:invoice#read'])->get('/invoices/{id}', /* ... */);

They work after keycloak.api, keycloak.web or auth:<keycloak guard>. Without a token they respond with 401, without the role/scope with 403.

docs.title: In code
docs.text:
use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Facades\Keycloak;

$token = Keycloak::token();

$token->hasRole('admin');
$token->hasAnyRole(['admin', 'editor']);
$token->hasAllRoles(['admin', 'auditor']);
$token->hasRealmRole('offline_access');
$token->hasClientRole('invoice-viewer', 'billing');

$token->realmRoles();            // ['admin', 'offline_access', ...]
$token->clientRoles();           // roles of the guard client(s)
$token->clientRoles('billing');
$token->allClientRoles();        // ['billing' => [...], 'account' => [...]]

$token->scopes();                // ['openid', 'email', 'orders:read']
$token->hasScope('orders:read');
$token->hasAnyScope(['a', 'b']);

$token->groups();                // ['/company/engineering']
$token->inGroup('engineering');  // matches "/company/engineering"

docs.title: Gates and policies
docs.text:
The package registers these abilities (disable with 'gates' => false):

Ability Arguments keycloak-role one or more roles (any) keycloak-roles one or more roles (all) keycloak-scope one or more scopes (any) keycloak-group a group name or path 
Gate::allows('keycloak-role', 'admin');
Gate::authorize('keycloak-role', ['admin', 'editor']);
$this->authorize('keycloak-scope', 'orders:write');   // in a controller

@can('keycloak-role', 'admin')
    <a href="/admin">Admin</a>
@endcan

can: middleware

Laravel's can:ability,arg middleware reads its arguments as route parameters or model classes, not as plain strings. Use keycloak.role:... for routes, and the gates in code and Blade.

Inside your own policies, use the token directly:

public function update(User $user, Invoice $invoice): bool
{
    return $user->hasRole('billing:invoice-editor') && $invoice->tenant_id === $user->tenant_id;
}

docs.title: Blade directives
docs.text:
@keycloakRole('admin', 'editor')
    <button>Publish</button>
@endkeycloakRole

@keycloakScope('orders:write')
    <button>New order</button>
@endkeycloakScope

docs.title: On the user model
docs.text:
Add HasKeycloakRoles to your user model (the bundled KCUserModel already has it):

use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Concerns\HasKeycloakRoles;

class User extends Authenticatable
{
    use HasKeycloakRoles;
}

$user->hasRole('admin');
$user->hasAnyRole(['admin', 'editor']);
$user->hasAllRoles([...]);
$user->hasRealmRole('...');
$user->hasClientRole('viewer', 'billing');
$user->hasScope('orders:read');
$user->inGroup('engineering');
$user->keycloakRoles();       // ['admin', ...]
$user->keycloakGroups();
$user->keycloakToken();       // KeycloakToken, or null when the current token belongs to someone else

The helpers only answer true when the current token belongs to this user (matched by keycloak_id), so checking roles of another user model returns false instead of leaking the caller's roles.

Stateless API users (KeycloakUser) have the same methods.

docs.title: UMA permissions (Authorization Services)
docs.text:
If you model resources, scopes and policies in Keycloak (Client → Authorization tab), ask Keycloak for a decision:

$oidc = Keycloak::oidc('api');

$oidc->checkPermission($token->jwt(), 'invoice#read');               // resource#scope
$oidc->checkPermission($token->jwt(), ['invoice#read', 'report']);   // all of them
$oidc->permissions($token->jwt());   // [['rsname' => 'invoice', 'scopes' => ['read']], ...]

Decisions are cached for token.introspection_cache_ttl seconds (default 30s) per token and permission set. The audience defaults to the guard's client_id (the resource server).

docs.title: 1.x KCAuth facade
docs.text:
The 1.x helpers still work and now read the current token:

use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Facades\KCAuth;

KCAuth::userRoles();
KCAuth::userRealmRoles();
KCAuth::userClientRoles();
KCAuth::hasAccess(['admin', Role::Editor]);
KCAuth::hasAccess(['editor'], inClientRoleOnly: true);

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: All options live in config/bhry98-keycloak.php (publish it with php artisan keycloak:install). Each option has a comment in the file. This page explains what they do.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
A guard is a named Keycloak realm + client pair. Everything in the package takes an optional guard name: Keycloak::oidc('api'), keycloak.api:api, Keycloak::users('web'), /auth/keycloak/login/web.

'default_guard' => env('KEYCLOAK_DEFAULT_GUARD', 'web'),

'guard' => [
    'web' => [
        'client_id' => env('KC_WEB_CLIENT_ID', env('KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID')),
        'client_secret' => env('KC_WEB_CLIENT_SECRET', env('KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET')),
        'realm' => env('KC_WEB_REALM', env('KEYCLOAK_REALM')),
        'redirect' => env('KC_WEB_REDIRECT_URI', env('KEYCLOAK_REDIRECT_URI')),
        'scopes' => ['openid', 'email', 'profile'],
    ],
    'api' => [ /* ... */ 'audience' => env('KC_API_AUDIENCE') ],
    'admin' => [ /* service account for the Admin API */ ],

    // Add as many as you need: one per frontend, tenant realm, partner...
    'partner-portal' => [
        'base_url' => 'https://sso.partner.test', // another Keycloak server
        'realm' => 'partners',
        'client_id' => 'portal',
        'client_secret' => env('PARTNER_SECRET'),
    ],
],
Key Description base_url Keycloak server URL. Defaults to the top-level base_url. realm, client_id, client_secret Realm and client credentials. Use an empty secret for public clients. redirect Callback URL for the browser login of this guard. scopes Scopes requested at login. audience String, comma-separated string, or array. When set, API tokens must name one of these in aud or azp. issuer Extra trusted issuer(s) for this guard (see Docker & Kubernetes). auth_guard The Laravel guard the browser login logs into (default: your default guard). redirect_after_logout Where Keycloak sends the browser after logout. provisioning true / false to override provisioning.enabled for this guard. role_clients Clients whose roles count for hasRole() (default: the guard's client_id + the token's azp).

Unknown guard names fall back to the top-level realm / client_id / client_secret.

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text:
'admin' => [
    'guard' => env('KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_GUARD', 'admin'), // whose credentials obtain the admin token
    'token_expiry_margin' => 30,                      // refresh admin / service tokens 30s early
],

The admin token is obtained once with client credentials and cached until shortly before it expires. A 401 from the Admin API refreshes it and retries the request once.

docs.title: Token validation
docs.text:
'token' => [
    'leeway' => 30,                     // clock-skew tolerance (seconds)
    'allowed_algs' => ['RS256', 'RS384', 'RS512', 'PS256', 'PS384', 'PS512', 'ES256', 'ES384', 'ES512', 'EdDSA'],
    'allowed_types' => ['Bearer'],      // rejects refresh and ID tokens used as access tokens
    'verify_issuer' => true,
    'issuer' => env('KEYCLOAK_ISSUER'), // public issuer when it differs from base_url
    'jwks_ttl' => 86400,                // realm public keys cache (seconds)
    'jwks_refresh_cooldown' => 30,      // min seconds between key re-downloads on unknown kid
    'introspection_cache_ttl' => 30,    // cache of introspection / UMA answers
],

Do not add none or HS* to allowed_algs

Keycloak signs access tokens with asymmetric keys. Allowing symmetric algorithms opens the door to algorithm-confusion attacks.

docs.title: Web SSO
docs.text:
'web' => [
    'pkce' => true,                 // PKCE (S256) on the authorization code flow
    'validation' => 'local',        // "local" (expiry check, no network) or "introspect" (cached)
    'refresh_tokens' => true,       // silently refresh with the refresh token
    'refresh_margin' => 15,         // refresh this many seconds before expiry
    'home' => '/',                  // redirect after login when there is no intended URL
],

See Web SSO → Session validation for the trade-offs.

docs.title: User provisioning
docs.text:
'users_model' => \Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Models\KCUserModel::class,

'provisioning' => [
    'enabled' => env('KEYCLOAK_PROVISIONING', true),
    'sync_ttl' => 300,  // skip the DB write while the claims are unchanged
    'attributes' => [   // column => claim (dot notation, or a closure)
        'keycloak_id' => 'sub',
        'email' => 'email',
        'username' => 'preferred_username',
        'first_name' => 'given_name',
        'last_name' => 'family_name',
        'name' => 'name',
        'avatar' => 'picture',
        'locale' => 'locale',
        'email_verified' => 'email_verified',
        // 'department' => 'attributes.department',
        // 'tenant_id' => fn ($token) => Tenant::idFor($token->claim('tenant')),
    ],
],

Use your own model by pointing users_model at it. It must have the columns you map and the keycloak_id column. Add the HasKeycloakRoles trait to it to get role helpers.

Closures in config

A closure in attributes stops php artisan config:cache from working. Use a custom resolver (Keycloak::resolveUserUsing()) instead if you cache your config.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
'roles' => [
    'clients' => null, // e.g. ['my-app', 'billing']; null = guard client_id + token azp
],

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
'cache' => [
    'store' => env('KEYCLOAK_CACHE_STORE'), // null = default store; Redis recommended in production
    'prefix' => 'bhry98_keycloak',
],

'http' => [
    'timeout' => 10,
    'connect_timeout' => 5,
    'retries' => 2,         // connection errors only, never on 4xx/5xx answers
    'retry_delay' => 100,   // ms
    'verify' => env('KEYCLOAK_VERIFY_SSL', true),
],

'routes' => [
    'enabled' => true,
    'prefix' => 'auth/keycloak',
    'middleware' => ['web'],
    'name' => 'keycloak.',
],

'migrations' => ['auto_load' => true],
'gates' => true, // keycloak-role / keycloak-scope gates and the @keycloakRole directive

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL – Keycloak server URL KEYCLOAK_REALM – Default realm KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID / KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET – Default client KEYCLOAK_REDIRECT_URI /auth/keycloak/callback Default login callback KEYCLOAK_RED_AFTER_LOGOUT APP_URL Post-logout redirect KEYCLOAK_DEFAULT_GUARD web Guard used when none is given KC_{WEB,API,ADMIN}_{CLIENT_ID,CLIENT_SECRET,REALM,REDIRECT_URI} defaults above Per-guard overrides KC_API_AUDIENCE – Required audience for API tokens KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_GUARD admin Credentials used for the Admin API KEYCLOAK_ISSUER – Public issuer URL KEYCLOAK_VERIFY_ISSUER true Check iss KEYCLOAK_TOKEN_LEEWAY 30 Clock skew (seconds) KEYCLOAK_JWKS_TTL 86400 Realm keys cache (seconds) KEYCLOAK_PKCE true PKCE on browser login KEYCLOAK_WEB_VALIDATION local local or introspect KEYCLOAK_HOME / Redirect after login KEYCLOAK_PROVISIONING true Sync users to the database KEYCLOAK_CACHE_STORE default Cache store KEYCLOAK_VERIFY_SSL true TLS verification

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: PHP 8.2 or newer, with ext-openssl and ext-json Laravel 11.x, 12.x or 13.x Keycloak 17 or newer (URLs without /auth). For older servers, put /auth in KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL.

docs.title: Install via Composer
docs.text:
composer require bhry98/keycloak-laravel-auth

The service provider and the Keycloak facade are auto-discovered.

php artisan keycloak:install      # publishes config/bhry98-keycloak.php and prints the .env keys
php artisan migrate               # adds the Keycloak columns to your users table

Users table

The bundled migration creates a users table, or, if your app already has one (Laravel's default migration), adds the Keycloak columns (keycloak_id, keycloak_realm, username, ...) and makes password nullable. To customise it, set migrations.auto_load to false and publish it: php artisan vendor:publish --tag=bhry98-keycloak-migrations.

You only need the table if you use the browser login or user provisioning. A pure API that uses stateless users needs no table at all.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The minimum for one realm and one client:

KEYCLOAK_BASE_URL=https://sso.example.com
KEYCLOAK_REALM=my-realm
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID=my-laravel-app
KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET=change-me
KEYCLOAK_REDIRECT_URI="${APP_URL}/auth/keycloak/callback/web"

Every guard (web, api, admin) falls back to these values. Override them per guard when you use different clients:

# Browser login client
KC_WEB_CLIENT_ID=my-web-app
KC_WEB_CLIENT_SECRET=...

# API resource server: tokens must be issued for this audience
KC_API_CLIENT_ID=orders-api
KC_API_AUDIENCE=orders-api

# Admin REST API service account (can live in another realm)
KC_ADMIN_REALM=my-realm
KC_ADMIN_CLIENT_ID=laravel-admin
KC_ADMIN_CLIENT_SECRET=...

Then check everything is reachable:

php artisan keycloak:check --admin

+-------+----------+----------------+------------------------------------------+-------------------+--------------------+
| Guard | Realm    | Client         | Discovery                                | JWKS              | Client credentials |
+-------+----------+----------------+------------------------------------------+-------------------+--------------------+
| web   | my-realm | my-web-app     | https://sso.example.com/realms/my-realm  | 1 signing key(s)  | ok                 |
| api   | my-realm | orders-api     | https://sso.example.com/realms/my-realm  | 1 signing key(s)  | ok                 |
| admin | my-realm | laravel-admin  | https://sso.example.com/realms/my-realm  | 1 signing key(s)  | ok                 |
+-------+----------+----------------+------------------------------------------+-------------------+--------------------+
Admin API token: ok

docs.title: Setting up Keycloak
docs.text:
Create the clients in your realm (Clients → Create client, type OpenID Connect).

Browser login (web)API (resource server)Admin API (service account)Password grant (optional) Setting Value Client authentication On (confidential) Standard flow On Valid redirect URIs https://your-app.test/auth/keycloak/callback/web Valid post logout redirect URIs https://your-app.test/* (or +) Web origins https://your-app.test Advanced → PKCE method S256 (optional, the package always sends it)

The API only verifies tokens, so it needs no flow enabled. To require that tokens are meant for your API, add an Audience mapper to the client that issues the tokens (your SPA / mobile app):

  1. Client scopes → Create orders-api-audience → Mappers → By configuration → Audience, included client audience: orders-api.
  2. Add the scope to the SPA client as a Default scope.
  3. Set KC_API_AUDIENCE=orders-api.

Enable Service accounts on this client if it also calls other services with Http::withKeycloakToken().

Setting Value Client authentication On Standard flow Off Service accounts roles On

Then in Service account roles → Assign role → Filter by clients, add the realm-management roles you need, for example manage-users, view-users, query-groups, view-clients or manage-realm.

For Keycloak::oidc()->password(), enable Direct access grants on the client. Prefer the browser flow for user-facing apps. The password grant is mainly useful for first-party mobile apps, CLIs and tests.

docs.title: Roles, groups and scopes in the token
docs.text: Keycloak puts realm roles in realm_access.roles and client roles in resource_access.<client>.roles by default (the roles client scope). For groups, add a Group Membership mapper (token claim name groups, Full group path on) to a client scope. See Authorization.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Browser app or admin panel: Web SSO
  • REST API or microservice: API authentication
  • Fine-tune behaviour: Configuration

docs.title: OIDC & service tokens
docs.text:
Keycloak::oidc($guard) gives you the OpenID Connect / OAuth 2 endpoints of a guard's realm and client. Token-endpoint methods return Keycloak's JSON answer as an array (access_token, expires_in, refresh_token, refresh_expires_in, id_token, token_type, scope, ...).

All calls share the package's HTTP settings (timeouts, retries on connection errors, TLS verification), and Http::fake() works with them in tests.

docs.title: Service-to-service calls
docs.text:
The most common backend need is calling another API as this service:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Http;

Http::withKeycloakToken()->get('https://orders.internal/api/orders');      // default guard
Http::withKeycloakToken('api')->post('https://billing.internal/api/invoices', $data);
Http::withKeycloakToken('api', 'billing:write')->post(/* ... */);           // with a scope

$token = Keycloak::serviceToken('api');   // the raw string

The token is obtained with the client credentials grant (enable Service accounts on the client) and cached until shortly before it expires (admin.token_expiry_margin). Every request, worker and server that shares the cache reuses it.

To call another service as the current user, forward their token:

Http::withKeycloakUserToken()->get('https://inventory.internal/api/stock');

docs.title: Token exchange
docs.text:
Trade the user's token for one issued to another client (RFC 8693). Token exchange must be enabled in Keycloak.

$tokens = Keycloak::oidc('api')->exchange($request->bearerToken(), audience: 'inventory-api');

Http::withToken($tokens['access_token'])->get('https://inventory.internal/api/stock');

docs.title: Password grant
docs.text:
Useful for first-party mobile apps, CLIs and tests. Requires Direct access grants on the client.

use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Exceptions\OidcException;

Route::post('/api/login', function (Request $request) {
    try {
        return Keycloak::oidc('api')->password($request->input('username'), $request->input('password'));
    } catch (OidcException $e) {
        // $e->error() === 'invalid_grant', $e->errorDescription(), $e->status()
        return response()->json(['message' => 'Invalid credentials'], 401);
    }
});

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text: $tokens = Keycloak::oidc('api')->refresh($refreshToken);

docs.title: Client credentials, code exchange
docs.text:
Keycloak::oidc('api')->clientCredentials('scope-a scope-b');         // uncached, full answer
Keycloak::oidc('web')->code($code, $redirectUri, $codeVerifier);     // custom frontends

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
Ask Keycloak whether a token is still active, for example for high-risk operations where you don't want to wait for the token to expire:

$result = Keycloak::oidc('api')->introspect($jwt);         // full RFC 7662 answer
$active = Keycloak::oidc('api')->isActive($jwt);           // cached for token.introspection_cache_ttl

docs.title: Userinfo
docs.text: $profile = Keycloak::oidc()->userInfo($accessToken);

docs.title: Logout and revocation
docs.text:
Keycloak::oidc('api')->logout($refreshToken);                 // end the Keycloak session (back-channel)
Keycloak::oidc('api')->revoke($refreshToken);                 // revoke a token
Keycloak::oidc('web')->logoutUrl($idToken, url('/'));         // front-channel logout URL for browsers

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Keycloak::oidc()->discovery();   // .well-known/openid-configuration, cached for a day

docs.title: UMA permissions
docs.text: See Authorization → UMA: checkPermission() and permissions().

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every failure raises a Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Exceptions\OidcException (a KeycloakException):

$e->status();            // HTTP status from Keycloak (0 when unreachable)
$e->error();             // OAuth error code, e.g. "invalid_grant"
$e->errorDescription();  // human readable reason
$e->response();          // Illuminate\Http\Client\Response|null

docs.title: Testing your application
docs.text:
Keycloak::fake() generates a local RSA key pair, makes every configured guard trust it, and signs real RS256 tokens. Your middleware, guards, role checks and provisioning run exactly as in production, and no Keycloak server is needed.

Add the trait to your base TestCase:

use Bhry98\KeycloakAuth\Testing\InteractsWithKeycloak;

abstract class TestCase extends BaseTestCase
{
    use InteractsWithKeycloak;
}

docs.title: API routes
docs.text:
it('lists orders for managers', function () {
    $this->actingAsKeycloakUser(['roles' => ['manager']])
        ->getJson('/api/orders')
        ->assertOk();
});

it('forbids plain users', function () {
    $this->actingAsKeycloakUser(['roles' => ['user']])
        ->getJson('/api/orders')
        ->assertForbidden();
});

it('needs a token', function () {
    $this->getJson('/api/orders')->assertUnauthorized();
});

Claim shortcuts:

Key Becomes roles realm_access.roles client_roles ['editor'] → roles of the guard client, or ['billing' => ['viewer']] scopes the space-separated scope claim anything else copied as-is (sub, email, groups, tenant, ...); null removes a default claim

Defaults include a random sub, email, preferred_username, names, typ: Bearer, the guard's client as azp, the correct iss and a 5-minute expiry.

$jwt = $this->keycloakToken(['sub' => $user->keycloak_id], guard: 'api');

$fake = Keycloak::fake();
$fake->token(['roles' => ['admin']], 'api', ttl: -60);  // an expired token
$fake->make([...]);                                    // a KeycloakToken object
$fake->tokenResponse([...]);                           // a token-endpoint style array
$fake->jwks();                                         // the public keys

docs.title: Web routes
docs.text:
it('shows the dashboard', function () {
    $user = User::factory()->create(['keycloak_id' => (string) Str::uuid()]);

    $this->actingAsKeycloakWebUser($user, ['roles' => ['admin']])
        ->get('/dashboard')
        ->assertOk();
});

docs.title: Keycloak HTTP calls
docs.text:
OIDC and Admin API calls go through Laravel's HTTP client, so Http::fake() works:

Http::fake([
    '*/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token' => Http::response(['access_token' => 'x', 'expires_in' => 60]),
    '*/admin/realms/my-realm/users' => Http::response(null, 201, ['Location' => '.../users/new-id']),
]);

expect(Keycloak::users()->create(['username' => 'jane']))->toBe('new-id');

docs.title: Artisan commands
docs.text:
Command What it does keycloak:install [--migrations] Publish the config (and migrations) and print the .env keys. keycloak:check [guard...] [--admin] For each guard: discovery document, realm keys, client credentials, and optionally an Admin API token. Exits non-zero on failure, which makes it usable as a deploy or readiness check. keycloak:decode {token} [--guard=] [--verify] Print subject, client, issuer, expiry, roles, scopes and all claims; --verify also checks signature, expiry, issuer and audience. keycloak:clear-cache Forget cached realm keys, discovery documents, admin and service tokens. 
php artisan keycloak:decode eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs... --guard=api --verify

docs.title: Events
Long-running workers (Octane, queues)
docs.text:
The package keeps resolved config, realm keys and recently verified tokens in memory for speed. The keycloak guard is reset for every request. After changing config at runtime, call:

Keycloak::forgetResolved();   // drop in-memory state
Keycloak::flushCache();       // also forget cached keys and tokens

docs.title: From 1.x to 2.0
docs.text:
2.0 is a rewrite, but the 1.x public API keeps working: config keys, routes, middleware aliases, KCAuth, KCUserModel, and the KeycloakUsersService, KeycloakRoleService, KeycloakGroupService and KeycloakJWTService classes.

composer require bhry98/keycloak-laravel-auth:^2.0
php artisan migrate          # safe to run; nothing changes for existing 1.x tables
php artisan keycloak:check

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• PHP 8.2+ and Laravel 11, 12 or 13.
  • creativeorange/gravatar is no longer required. avatar_url builds the Gravatar URL itself. Remove the package if nothing else uses it.

docs.title: Behaviour changes to review

Set KEYCLOAK_WEB_VALIDATION=introspect to keep server-side checks (now cached). keycloak.api verified the token, $request->user() was empty also resolves the user (provisioned or stateless) Set KEYCLOAK_PROVISIONING=false to keep APIs database-free. keycloak.api failure body {"error": "..."} same, plus message when APP_DEBUG=true none Logout redirected to Keycloak, user stayed there RP-initiated logout, user returns to redirect_after_logout Add the URL to Valid post logout redirect URIs. docs.text:
// Before
$jwt = (new KeycloakJWTService)->validateAndDecode($token);
$roles = KCAuth::userRoles();
(new KeycloakRoleService)->assignRoleToUser($userId, 'editor');

// After
$token = Keycloak::check($token, 'api');
$roles = Keycloak::token()->roles();
Keycloak::users()->assignRealmRoles($userId, ['editor']);

  • Replace VerifyKeycloakTokenForAgent / VerifyKeycloakTokenForApiAgent with keycloak.api.
  • Replace hand-written Http::withToken(...) service calls with Http::withKeycloakToken().
